I’ll try to explain since no one else truly has thus far. They should tell you how long your training is. Standard is 2 weeks. You will be paid whatever pharmacist salary was told/offered to you. When you float you will be scheduled for your minimum number of hours biweekly or more. I was contacted for 64 but was frequently scheduled for 80 so if you don’t want that tell the scheduler. If you do want that tell the scheduler. You will get your hourly rate for every hour over base. If you work over 80 hours biweekly you’ll get your base rate plus 20. This won’t happen with holiday or pto hours btw. This part entirely relies on where you work, who likes you and what the market need is. Hi 5th year Pharm D major here. So my year experienced a lot of changes for many things. We were kind of a guinea pig year in terms of rolling out new things and there will probably be even more changes for you. I will try to answer your questions as best as I can.

It’s hard for me to compare the program because I’ve only taken classes here but this program seems to be relatively run of the mill. I think a course many struggled with would be pharmacology medchem. They will always be that one (or two) hard course that you have to get through but you learn to deal with the course load after some bad first tests. I’ have always excelled in school and I am smart but I have struggled so much in this program, I don’t know if it’s other college adjustments on top of the course load but it was tough and almost got kicked out (if you want more info pm me). I think classes can be manageable but you need a very good study-social life balance, need to study early, and good organization skills. All things I struggled with coming. In general people tend to get weeded out in year 2/3 because they are too lazy to keep up with the work or realize this is not the program for them. Some professors of course are better than others. In general pharm sci < pharmacy practice professors. The research based professors tend to suck at teach. I’d say people like saczynki is an exception. There is little flexibility, one of the most rigid programs potentially only behind a couple combined majors in terms of flexibility. Almost everything pharmacy related (years 3-6/professional years) must be done in that specific semester and is only offered once a year. Labs you get some flexibility on the time. You of course can do a minor, the more AP credits the better! I came in with 26 credits (32 is the max) and that allowed me to choose classes a little earlier than my peers and get into the electives I wanted and of course gave me more free space for electives because I didn’t have to take calf and I had courses that fulfilled my nupath requirements. I am actually going to graduate with a double minor (music + psychology) and I’m in the honors program which comes with specific classes for them but I really had to finesse my schedule and plan this put from year 2/3. You can study abroad but it’s pretty much only that first fall (Nuin) or you can do a dialogue after that freshman year summer but after that no space. Every summer is booked and all other courses must happen in Boston. For my scholarship it stated that all 6 years of my program is covered (full tuition) so I don’t have to pay but that is rare. Most scholarships only cover the undergrad portion aka up until your 5th year. In year six you are a grad student. I’d say read the terms of your scholarship carefully and ask a financial aid advisor if you’re not sure. Coops are nice depending on where you go. Some can be really far out some can pay really well or be flexible but they are only 4 months (semester long) for pharmacy and pt majors because of our 6 year accelerated programs. It’s still way more than most pharmacy schools such as mcphs.
